\section{Proofs and Derivations\label{sec_apdx:Proofs-and-Derivations}}

\subsubsection*{Changes in Aggregate Price Indexes}

Combining the cost function in Section \ref{sec:Theoretical-Analysis}
with Equations (\ref{eq:lambda_ijk}) and (\ref{eq: consumption tax}),
the change in the price index of the industry $k$ composite is:
\[
\hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,k}=\hat{\tau}_{i,k}\,\hat{w}^{\left(\alpha^{L}_{i,k}+\alpha^{R}_{i,k}\right)}_{i}\hat{\ell}^{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}_{i,k}\hat{\lambda}^{\frac{1}{\sigma_{k}-1}}_{ii,k}\prod_{g\in\mathbb{G}}\hat{\tilde{P}}^{\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}}_{i,g}.
\]
Taking logs from the above equation and writing it in vector notation,
yields
\[
\ln\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{i}=\ln\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}_{i}}+\left(\textbf{I}-\textbf{A}_{i}\right)\textbf{1}\,\ln w_{i}+\textbf{B}_{i}+\textbf{A}_{i}\ln\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{i}
\]
where $\textbf{A}_{i}=\left[\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}\right]_{k,g}$ is the
$K\times K$ input-output matrix; $\textbf{B}_{i}\equiv\left[\alpha^{R}_{i,k}\ln\hat{\ell}_{i,k}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{k}-1}\ln\lambda_{ii,k}\right]_{k}$
is a $K\times1$ vector; and $\textbf{1 }$ and $\textbf{I}$ are
respectively $K\times1$ column vector of ones and the $K\times K$
identity matrix. Inverting the above equation, delivers:
\[
\ln\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{i}=\textbf{1}\,\ln w_{i}+\left(\textbf{I}-\textbf{A}_{i}\right)^{-1}\left[\ln\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}_{i}}+\textbf{B}_{i}\right]
\]
Letting $a_{i,gk}$ denote the entry $\left(k,g\right)$ of the inverse
Leontief matrix, the above equation delivers the following expression
for the change in the industry-level price index:
\[
\hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,k}=\hat{w}_{i}\times\prod_{g\in\mathbb{G}}\left(\hat{\lambda}^{\frac{a_{i,gk}}{\sigma_{g}-1}}_{ii,g}\right)\times\prod_{k'\in\mathbb{E}}\left(\hat{\tau}^{a_{i,k'k}}_{i,k'}\right)\times\prod_{k'\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}\left(\hat{\ell}^{\alpha^{R}_{i,k'}a_{i,k'k}}_{i,k'}\right)
\]


\paragraph*{Change in Industrial Emissions.}

To characterize the change in industrial emissions, $\hat{Z}^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}$,
we appeal to the proportionality condition, $Z_{i,gk}=v_{i,gk}C_{i,gk}$,
which links emissions for each energy transaction to the quantity
of energy inputs, where the conversion factor, $v_{i,gk}$, is an
engineering constant. Considering the Cobb-Douglas production function
with country and industry-specific weights, we can specify the unit
input cost as
\[
c_{i,k}=w^{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}_{i}r^{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}_{i,k}\,\prod_{g\in\mathbb{G}}\left(\tilde{P}^{\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}}_{i,g}\right),
\]
Note that the share of reserves in production is only non-zero in
primary energy sectors and zero otherwise, i.e., $\alpha^{R}_{i,k}>0$
if $k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}$ and $\alpha^{R}_{i,k}=0$ for all $k\notin\mathbb{E}_{1}$.
The intermediate input price index, $\tilde{P}_{i,g}=\left(1+t^{\left(I\right)}_{i,g}\right)P_{i,g}$,
is the after-tax price of input bundle $g$, where the tax $t^{\left(c\right)}_{i,g}$
is revised only for energy inputs ($g\in\mathbb{E}$). Based on cost
minimization,
\[
Z^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}=v^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}C^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}=v_{i,gk}\frac{\alpha^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}}{\tilde{P}_{i,g}}\,\frac{w_{i}\ell_{i,k}L_{i}}{\alpha^{\left(L\right)}_{i,k}}.
\]
Given the constancy of $v^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}$, $\alpha^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}$,
$\alpha^{\left(L\right)}_{i,k}$, and $L_{i}$, we can use the above
equation to specify the change in industrial emissions as

\[
\hat{Z}^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}=\hat{C}^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}=\hat{\ell}_{i,k}\left(\frac{\hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,g}}{\hat{w}_{i}}\right)^{-1},\qquad\qquad\left(\forall g\in\mathbb{E},\ k\in\mathbb{K}\right)
\]
The above equation equates the change in emissions associated with
energy use in a given industry with the changes in the relative price
of energy to labor inputs, $\hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,g}/\hat{w}_{i}$, and
the change in employment $\hat{\ell}_{i,k}$.

Next, we must characterize the change in the relative price of labor-to-energy
in terms of changes in observable share variables. Invoking the constant
elasticity import demand system, $\lambda_{ii,g}=\left((1+t^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,g})P_{ii,g}/P_{i,g}\right)^{1-\sigma_{k}}$,
we can write the change in the after-tax price $\tilde{P}_{i,k}=(1+t^{\left(I\right)}_{i,k})P_{i,k}$
of the energy composite as
\[
\hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,g}=\hat{\tau}^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,g}\,\hat{\tau}^{(C)}_{i,g}\,\hat{P}_{ii,g}\hat{\lambda}^{\frac{1}{\sigma_{g}-1}}_{ii,g}
\]
Considering our parametric specification for $c_{i,k}$, the change
in the producer price of the variety $(i,i,k)$ in response to the
policy shocks is
\begin{align*}
\hat{P}_{ii,k}=\hat{c}_{i,k} & =\hat{w}^{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}_{i}\,\hat{r}^{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}_{i}\,\prod_{g\in\mathbb{G}}\hat{\tilde{P}}^{\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}}_{i,g}\\
 & =\hat{w}^{\left(\alpha^{L}_{i,k}+\alpha^{R}_{i,k}\right)}_{i}\,\hat{\ell}^{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}_{i,k}\,\prod_{g\in\mathbb{G}}\hat{\tilde{P}}^{\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}}_{i,g},
\end{align*}
where the last line follows from cost minimization, whereby $r_{i,k}R_{i,k}=\alpha^{R}_{i,k}w_{i}\ell_{i,k}L_{i}/\alpha^{L}_{i,k}$,
which yields $\hat{r}_{i,k}=\hat{w}_{i}\hat{\ell}_{i,k}$ given the
constancy of $\alpha^{R}_{i,k},$$\alpha^{L}_{i,k}$, and $R_{i,k}$.
To make the notation more compact, we integrate the carbon policy
change, which channels through changes to energy-specific consumption
and supply-side taxes as
\[
\hat{\tau}_{i,k}\equiv\hat{\tau}^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,g}\,\hat{\tau}^{(C)}_{i,g}
\]
Appealing to the expression for $\hat{P}_{ii,k}$ and using the compact
notation for energy taxes, we can specify the change in the after-tax
price of composite energy input $k\in\mathbb{E}$ as
\[
\hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,k}=\hat{\tau}_{i,k}\,\hat{w}^{\left(\alpha^{L}_{i,k}+\alpha^{R}_{i,k}\right)}_{i}\hat{\ell}^{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}_{i}\hat{\lambda}^{\frac{1}{\sigma_{k}-1}}_{ii,k}\prod_{g\in\mathbb{G}}\hat{\tilde{P}}^{\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}}_{i,g}\,.
\]
The system of equations specified above implicitly determines $\left\{ \hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,k}\right\} _{k}$
in terms of $\left\{ \hat{w}_{i},\hat{r}_{i},\hat{\tau}_{i,k},\hat{\ell}_{i,k},\hat{\lambda}_{ii,k}\right\} $.
Inverting this system and performing some algebraic simplifications
yields
\[
\hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,k}=\hat{w}_{i}\times\prod_{g\in\mathbb{G}}\left(\hat{\lambda}^{\frac{a_{i,gk}}{\sigma_{g}-1}}_{ii,g}\right)\times\prod_{k'\in\mathbb{E}}\left(\hat{\tau}^{a_{i,k'k}}_{i,k'}\right)\times\prod_{k'\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}\left(\hat{\ell}^{\alpha^{R}_{i,k'}a_{i,k'k}}_{i,k'}\right)
\]
Rearranging the above equation specified the $\hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,k}/w_{i}$
for each energy variety, which when plugged back into our initial
expression for $\hat{Z}^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}$, yields
\begin{equation}
\hat{Z}^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}=\hat{\ell}_{i,k}\times\underbrace{\prod_{k\in\mathbb{G}}\left(\hat{\lambda}^{\frac{a_{i,kg}}{1-\sigma_{k}}}_{ii,k}\right)}_{\text{trade-related effects}}\times\overbrace{\underbrace{\prod_{k'\in\mathbb{E}}\left(\hat{\tau}^{-a_{i,k'g}}_{i,k'}\right)}_{\text{carbon policy}}\times\underbrace{\prod_{k'\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}\hat{\ell}^{-\alpha^{R}_{i,k'}a_{i,k'g}}_{i,k'}}_{\text{extraction price}}}^{\text{domestic economy adjustments}}\qquad\qquad\left(\forall g\in\mathbb{E}\right)\label{eq: Z_hat (industrial) appendix}
\end{equation}
To give intuition, the term labelled as ``trade-related effects''
encompasses the information about how trade impacts the relative price
of labor-to-energy inputs via the domestic expenditure shares. The
remaining three terms represent adjustments to domestic variables.
All these effects are adjusted by the role of input-output linkages.
Also note that since energy production uses non-energy inputs, adjustment
to non-energy prices influence the price of energy inputs.

\subsubsection*{Changes in Income to Wage Ratio}

Total income in country $i$ is the sum of primary factor rewards
and energy tax revenues. Namely,
\[
Y_{i}=w_{i}L_{i}+\sum_{k}r_{i,k}R_{i,k}+\sum_{k}\left[(\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}-1)P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}\right]+\sum_{k}\frac{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\left[\beta_{i,k}Y_{i}+\sum_{g}\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}P_{ii,g}Q_{i,g}\right]
\]
Rearranging the above equation yields
\[
Y_{i}=\frac{w_{i}L_{i}+\sum_{k}r_{i,k}R_{i,k}+\sum_{k}\left[(\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}-1)P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}\right]+\left[\sum_{k}\frac{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\sum_{g}\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}P_{ii,g}Q_{i,g}\right]}{1-\sum_{k}\frac{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\beta_{i,k}}
\]
Next we specify industry-wide sales in terms of wage payments, by
noting that 
\[
r_{i,k}R_{i,k}=\frac{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}w_{i}\ell_{i,k}L_{i},\qquad\qquad P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}=\frac{1}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}w_{i}\ell_{i,k}L_{i}.
\]
Based on the above equation, we can express the payments to energy
reserves as
\[
\sum_{k}r_{i,k}R_{i,k}=\sum_{k}\left[\frac{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}\ell_{i,k}\right]w_{i}L_{i}
\]
and the energy tax income as
\begin{align*}
\sum_{k}\left[(\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}-1)P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}\right]+ & \left[\sum_{k}\frac{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\sum_{g}\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}P_{ii,g}Q_{i,g}\right]\\
= & \left(\sum_{k}\left[(\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}-1)\frac{\ell_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}\right]+\left[\sum_{k}\frac{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\sum_{g}\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}\frac{\ell_{i,g}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,g}}\right]\right)w_{i}L_{i}.
\end{align*}
Plugging the above equations back into our last expression for $Y_{i}$
yields
\[
Y_{i}=\frac{1+\sum_{k}\left[\frac{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}\ell_{i,k}+(\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}-1)\frac{\ell_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}+\frac{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\sum_{g}\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}\frac{\ell_{i,g}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,g}}\right]}{1-\sum_{k}\frac{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\beta_{i,k}}w_{i}L_{i},
\]
which immediately implies the expression for the income to wage ratio
presented in the main text:
\begin{align*}
\kappa_{i}\equiv\frac{Y_{i}}{w_{i}L_{i}} & =\frac{1+\sum_{k}\left(\alpha^{R}_{i,k}+(\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}-1)+\sum_{g}\frac{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}\right)\frac{\ell_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}}{1-\sum_{k}\frac{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\beta_{i,k}}.\\
 & =\frac{1+\sum_{k}\left(-\alpha^{L}_{i,k}+\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}-\sum_{g}\frac{\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\right)\frac{\ell_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}}{1-\sum_{k}\frac{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\beta_{i,k}}=\frac{\sum_{k}\left(\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}-\sum_{g}\frac{\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\right)\frac{\ell_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}}{\sum_{k}\frac{\beta_{i,k}}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}}
\end{align*}
The change in the income-to-wage ratio starting from a baseline of
zero taxes, follows immediately from the fact that $\alpha^{R}_{i,k}$,
$\alpha^{L}_{i,k}$, and $\beta_{i,k}$ are constant implying that
\[
\kappa'_{i}=\frac{\sum_{k}\left(\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}-\sum_{g}\frac{\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\right)\frac{\ell_{i,k}\hat{\ell}_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}}{\sum_{k}\frac{\beta_{i,k}}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}},\qquad\qquad\kappa{}_{i}\mid_{\boldsymbol{\tau}=1}=1+\sum\frac{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}\ell_{i,k},
\]
which in turn delivers the expression for $\hat{\kappa}_{i}$ presented
in the main text:
\[
\hat{\kappa}_{i}\equiv\frac{\kappa'_{i}}{\kappa_{i}}=\frac{\sum_{k}\left(\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}-\sum_{g}\frac{\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}\right)\frac{\ell_{i,k}\hat{\ell}_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}}{\left(1+\sum\frac{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}\ell_{i,k}\right)\sum_{k}\frac{\beta_{i,k}}{\tau^{(C)}_{i,k}}}
\]


\subsubsection*{Consumption Effects of Carbon Pricing Reform}

Our goal is to characterize the effect of the carbon tax shock, $\left\{ d\ln\tau^{(C)}_{i,k},d\ln\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}\right\} _{k}$,
on real consumption $C_{i}=\text{V}_{i}\left(Y_{i},\tilde{\boldsymbol{P}}_{i}\right)$.
Here, $Y_{i}$ denotes income, which is the sum of factor rewards
and tax revenues. In particular,
\begin{equation}
Y_{i}=\tilde{w}_{i}L_{i}+\sum_{k}(\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}-1)P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}+\sum_{k}(\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}-1)P_{i,k}C_{i,k}\label{eq: Y_i (appendix -- energy tax)}
\end{equation}
where $C_{i,k}\equiv C^{\left(H\right)}_{i,k}+\sum_{g}C^{\left(I\right)}_{i,kg}$
and $\tilde{w}_{i}L_{i}$ is a short-hand for primary factor compensation,
which includes labor and energy reserves. Taking derivatives from
$C_{i}=\text{V}_{i}\left(Y_{i},\tilde{\boldsymbol{P}}_{i}\right)$,
yields
\[
\text{d}C_{i}=\frac{\partial\text{V}_{i}\left(.\right)}{\partial Y_{i}}\text{d}Y_{i}+\sum_{k}\sum_{n}\frac{\partial\text{V}_{i}\left(.\right)}{\partial\ln\tilde{P}_{ni,k}}\text{d\ensuremath{\ln}}\tilde{P}_{ni,k},
\]
Since $\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}$ is applied to all demanded goods
in industry $k$, the change in the variety-specific price $\text{d\ensuremath{\ln}}\tilde{P}_{ni,k}$
can be expressed as
\[
\text{d\ensuremath{\ln}}\tilde{P}_{ni,k}=\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}+\text{d\ensuremath{\ln}}P_{ni,k}.
\]
Plugging the above equation back into the welfare expression, delivers
\[
\text{d}C_{i}=\frac{\partial\text{V}_{i}\left(.\right)}{\partial Y_{i}}\text{d}Y_{i}+\sum_{k}\sum_{n}\frac{\partial\text{V}_{i}\left(.\right)}{\partial\ln\tilde{P}_{ni,k}}\left(\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}+\text{d\ensuremath{\ln}}P_{ni,k}\right).
\]
We can invoke Roy's identity $\frac{\partial\text{V}_{i}\left(.\right)}{\partial\tilde{P}_{ni,k}}=\frac{\partial\text{V}_{i}\left(.\right)}{\partial Y_{i}}C^{\left(H\right)}_{ni,k}$
to simplify this equation as
\begin{align*}
\text{d}C_{i} & =\frac{\partial\text{V}_{i}\left(.\right)}{\partial Y_{i}}\left[\text{d}Y_{i}-\sum_{k}\sum_{n}P_{ni,k}C^{\left(H\right)}_{ni,k}\left(\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}+\text{d\ensuremath{\ln}}P_{ni,k}\right)\right]\\
 & =\frac{\partial\text{V}_{i}\left(.\right)}{\partial Y_{i}}\left[\text{d}Y_{i}-Y_{i}\sum_{k}\sum_{n}\beta_{i,k}\lambda_{ni,k}\left(\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}+\text{d\ensuremath{\ln}}\tilde{P}_{ni,k}\right)\right]
\end{align*}
To further simplify the above equation, we note that $\text{d}\ln P_{ni,k}=\text{d}\ln\tilde{P}_{ii,k}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{k}-1}\left(\text{d}\ln\lambda_{ni,k}-\text{d}\ln\lambda_{ii,k}\right)$,
and follow the ACR logic to write the above equation as
\begin{equation}
\text{d}C_{i}=\frac{\partial\text{V}_{i}\left(.\right)}{\partial Y_{i}}\left[\text{d}Y_{i}-Y_{i}\sum_{k}\beta_{i,k}\left(\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}+\text{d}\ln\tilde{P}_{ii,k}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{k}-1}\text{d}\ln\lambda_{ii,k}\right)\right]\label{eq: dC_i (1 appendix -- energy tax )}
\end{equation}
Noting that $\tilde{P}_{ii,k}=\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}P_{ii,k}$,
we can specify domestic price changes as
\[
\text{d}\ln\tilde{P}_{ii,k}=\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}+\alpha^{(\tilde{L})}_{i,k}d\ln\tilde{w}_{i}+\sum_{g}\alpha^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}\text{d}\ln\tilde{P}_{i,g},
\]
where $\alpha^{(\tilde{L})}_{i,k}\equiv\left[1-\sum_{g}\alpha^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}\right]$
denotes the primary factor input share. Considering that $\tilde{P}_{i,g}=\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,g}\,\tilde{P}_{ii,g}\lambda^{\frac{1}{\sigma_{g}-1}}_{ii,g}$
can be reformulated as
\[
\text{d}\ln\tilde{P}_{ii,k}=\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}+\alpha^{(\tilde{L})}_{i,k}d\ln\tilde{w}_{i}+\sum_{g}\alpha^{\left(I\right)}_{i,gk}\left(\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,g}+\text{d}\ln\tilde{P}_{ii,g}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{g}-1}\text{d}\ln\lambda_{ii,g}\right)
\]
The above equation can be alternatively represented in vector notation
as
\[
\text{d}\ln\tilde{\boldsymbol{P}}_{ii}=\text{d}\ln\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\left(Q\right)}_{i}+\left(\textbf{I}-\textbf{A}_{i}\right)\textbf{1}\text{d}\ln\tilde{w}_{i}+\textbf{A}_{i}\left(\text{d}\ln\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\left(C\right)}_{i}+\text{d}\ln\tilde{\boldsymbol{P}}_{ii}+\frac{1}{\sigma-1}\circ\text{d}\ln\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{ii}\right)
\]
Inverting the above system we get
\begin{equation}
\text{d}\ln\tilde{P}_{ii,k}=\text{d}\ln\tilde{w}_{i}+\sum_{g}a_{i,gk}\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,g}+\sum_{g}\tilde{a}_{i,gk}\left[\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,g}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{g}-1}d\ln\lambda_{ii,g}\right]\label{eq: dlnP_ii (appendix - energy tax)}
\end{equation}
where $a_{i,gk}$ is the element $\left(k,g\right)$ of the inverse
Leontief $\left(\textbf{I}-\textbf{A}_{i}\right)^{-1}$ and $\tilde{a}_{i,gk}$
is the element $\left(k,g\right)$ of the matrix $\left(I-\textbf{A}_{i}\right)^{-1}\textbf{A}_{i}$.
Noting that $\left(\textbf{I}-\textbf{A}_{i}\right)^{-1}\textbf{A}_{i}=\left(\textbf{I}-\textbf{A}_{i}\right)^{-1}-\textbf{I}$,
we get
\[
\tilde{a}_{i,kg}=\begin{cases}
a_{i,kg}-1 & k=g\\
a_{i,kg} & k\neq g
\end{cases},
\]
Considering the above equation, we can plug Equation \ref{eq: dlnP_ii (appendix - energy tax)}
into Equation \ref{eq: dC_i (1 appendix -- energy tax )} to obtain:
\begin{equation}
\text{d}C_{i}=\frac{\partial\text{V}_{i}\left(.\right)}{\partial Y_{i}}\left[\text{d}Y_{i}-Y_{i}\left\{ \text{d}\ln\tilde{w}_{i}+\sum_{k}\sum_{g}a_{i,kg}\beta_{i,g}\left(\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}+\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{k}-1}\text{d}\ln\lambda_{ii,k}\right)\right\} \right].\label{eq: dC_i (2 appendix -- energy tax)}
\end{equation}
Next we characterize the change in income by taking derivative from
Equation \ref{eq: Y_i (appendix -- energy tax)}, which delivers
\begin{align*}
\text{d}Y_{i}=\tilde{w}_{i}L_{i}\text{d}\ln w_{i} & +\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}}\left[\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}+(\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}-1)\frac{\partial\left(P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}\right)}{\partial\ln\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}}\right]d\ln\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}\\
 & +\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}}\left[\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}P_{i,k}C_{i,k}+(\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}-1)\frac{\partial\left(P_{i,k}C_{i,k}\right)}{\partial\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}}\right]d\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}
\end{align*}
In the neighborhood of $\boldsymbol{\tau}=1$, the above equation
simplifies to
\[
\text{d}Y_{i}\mid_{\boldsymbol{t}=0}=Y_{i}\text{d}\ln w_{i}+\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}}\left[P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}d\ln\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}\right]+\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}}\left[P_{ii,k}C_{i,k}d\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}\right]
\]
To evaluate the above equation, we use the market clearing condition
whereby total expenditure on good $k$ equals the final demand expenditure
$P_{i,k}C^{H}_{i,k}=\beta_{i,k}Y_{i}$ and the intermediate input
expenditure. Namely,
\[
P_{i,k}C_{i,k}=\beta_{i,k}Y_{i}+\sum_{g}\alpha^{\left(I\right)}_{i,kg}P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}
\]
 In a closed economy, the sales equals expenditure per industry, $P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}=P_{i,k}C_{i,k}$.
Hence, we can write the above equation in vector notation as $\boldsymbol{P}_{ii}\circ\boldsymbol{Q}_{i}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i}Y_{i}+\textbf{A}^{T}_{i}\boldsymbol{P}_{ii}\circ\boldsymbol{Q}_{i}$,
which after basic inversion implies:
\[
\frac{P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}}{Y_{i}}=\frac{P_{i,k}C_{i,k}}{Y_{i}}=\sum_{g}a_{i,kg}\beta_{i,g}\qquad\qquad\left[\text{closed economy}\right]
\]
The open economy counterpart of this equation can be stated as
\[
P_{i,k}C_{i,k}=\beta_{i,k}Y_{i}+\sum_{g}\alpha^{\left(I\right)}_{i,kg}P_{i,g}C_{i,g}+\sum_{g}\alpha^{\left(I\right)}_{i,kg}\mathcal{X}_{i,g}
\]
where $\mathcal{X}_{i,k}\equiv P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}-P_{i,k}C_{i,k}$ is
net exports in industry $k$. In vector notation, $\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\circ\boldsymbol{C}_{i}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i}Y_{i}+\textbf{A}^{T}_{i}\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\circ\boldsymbol{C}_{i}+\textbf{A}^{T}_{i}\boldsymbol{X}_{i}$,
which after inversion yields:
\[
\frac{P_{i,k}C_{i,k}}{Y_{i}}=\sum_{g}a_{i,kg}\beta_{i,g}+\sum_{g}\tilde{a}_{i,kg}\frac{\mathcal{X}_{i,g}}{Y_{i}}
\]
Alternatively, we can write the accounting equation as $P_{i,k}Q_{ii,k}=\mathcal{X}_{i,k}+\beta_{i,k}Y_{i}+\sum_{g}\alpha^{\left(I\right)}_{i,kg}P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}$,
which after inversion delivers
\[
\frac{P_{ii,k}Q_{i,k}}{Y_{i}}=\sum_{g}a_{i,kg}\beta_{i,g}+\sum_{g}a_{i,kg}\frac{\mathcal{X}_{i,g}}{Y_{i}}.
\]
Plugging the expressions for $\frac{P_{i,k}C_{i,k}}{Y_{i}}$ and $\frac{P_{i,k}Q_{ii,k}}{Y_{i}}$
into the equation representing $\text{d}Y_{i}\mid_{\boldsymbol{\tau}=1}$,
we obtain:
\[
\text{d}Y_{i}\mid_{\boldsymbol{\tau}=1}=Y_{i}\left\{ \text{d}\ln w_{i}+\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}}\sum_{g}\left[\left(a_{i,kg}\beta_{i,g}+a_{i,kg}\frac{\mathcal{X}_{i,g}}{Y_{i}}\right)d\ln\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}+\left(a_{i,kg}\beta_{i,g}+\tilde{a}_{i,kg}\frac{\mathcal{X}_{i,g}}{Y_{i}}\right)d\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}\right]\right\} 
\]
Plugging the above expression for $\text{d}Y_{i}$ into the Equation
\ref{eq: dC_i (2 appendix -- energy tax)} delivers:
\[
\text{d}C_{i}\mid_{\boldsymbol{\tau}=1}=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}}\sum_{g\in\mathbb{G}}\frac{\mathcal{X}_{i,g}}{Y_{i}}\left[a_{i,kg}\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(Q\right)}_{i,k}+\tilde{a}_{i,kg}\text{d}\ln\tau^{\left(C\right)}_{i,k}\right]+\sum_{g\in\mathbb{G}}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{G}}\frac{a_{i,kg}\beta_{i,g}}{1-\sigma_{k}}\text{d}\ln\lambda_{ii,k}
\]


\subsubsection*{Correlation between the consumption gains and emission gains from
trade}

This appendix establishes the claim under Remark 1. We use the following
notation for cross-country moments: $\mathbb{E}_{i}[\cdot]\equiv N^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}(\cdot)$,
and $\operatorname{Cov}_{i}(\widehat{C}_{i},\widehat{Z}_{i})\equiv\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}\widehat{Z}_{i}]-\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}]\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}_{i}].$
Apply the simplifying restrictions stated under Remark 1. Since the
reform changes only trade costs, all carbon-tax terms in Propositions
1 and 2 equal one. Since $\alpha^{R}_{0}=0$, the extraction price
terms also collapse to one. Moreover, national income equals labor
income, so the income-to-wage term in Proposition 2 becomes $\widehat{\kappa}_{i}=1$.
Finally, the proportionality assumption about emission intensities
neutralizes the composition term involving the weighted sum in Proposition
1. Under internationally symmetric input-output coefficients and final
expenditure shares, Propositions 1 and 2 give
\begin{equation}
\widehat{Z}_{i}=\prod_{k\in\mathbb{G}}\widehat{\lambda}^{\frac{a^{Z}_{k}}{1-\sigma_{k}}}_{ii,k}=\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a}^{Z}).\qquad\qquad\widehat{C}_{i}=\prod_{k\in\mathbb{G}}\widehat{\lambda}^{\frac{a^{C}_{k}}{1-\sigma_{k}}}_{ii,k}=\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C}).\label{eq:app-Z-special}
\end{equation}
where $a^{Z}_{k}\equiv a_{k0}$ and $a^{C}_{k}=\sum_{g}a_{kg}\beta_{g}$.
The operator $\Lambda_{i}(.)$ has two elementary properties that
will be useful going forward: $\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{0})=1,$ and
$\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a}+\boldsymbol{a'})=\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a'})$.
Lastly, define the Cauchy--Schwarz divergence $D_{\lambda}$ in trade
exposure under any two dependence vectors $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{a'}$
and the normalized divergence $\mathcal{D}_{\lambda}$ as
\begin{equation}
D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{a'})\equiv\ln\!\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})^{2}]\,\mathbb{E}_{i}[\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a'})^{2}]}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a'})]^{2}}\right],\qquad\qquad\mathcal{D}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{a}')\equiv\frac{D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{a}')}{D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{0})+D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}',\boldsymbol{0})}.\label{eq:main-DCS}
\end{equation}
Define the vector $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{a})\equiv\bigl(\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})\bigr)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$
that stacks all country-level exposure operators and define the following
cross-country operators for the inner product as $\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle_{i}\equiv\mathbb{E}_{i}[x_{i}y_{i}]$,
and the norm as $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_{i}\equiv\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{i}[x^{2}_{i}]}$
. The cosine similarity between in trade exposure for dependence profiles
$\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{a'}$ is
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{cos}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{a'})\equiv\frac{\langle\boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}),\boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{a'})\rangle_{i}}{\|\boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{a})\|_{i}\|\boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{a'})\|_{i}}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a'})]}{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})^{2}]\mathbb{E}_{i}[\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a'})^{2}]}}.\label{eq:app-cosine}
\end{equation}
Because $\Lambda_{i}(.)$ is strictly positive, the cosine lies in
$(0,1]$. The Cauchy--Schwarz divergence in (\ref{eq:main-DCS})
can equivalently be written as $D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{a'})=-2\ln\!\left[\operatorname{cos}^{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{a'})\right]$.
Moreover, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality implies $\mathbb{E}_{i}[\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a'})]^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}_{i}[\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})^{2}]\mathbb{E}_{i}[\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a'})^{2}]$,
so the divergence is non-negative: $D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{a'})\geq0$.

Next, we characterize $\operatorname{Cov}_{i}(\widehat{C}_{i},\widehat{Z}_{i})$
in terms of Cauchy--Schwarz divergence. To this end, we note first
that both $\widehat{C}_{i}$ and $\widehat{Z}_{i}$ are strictly positive.
Evaluating (\ref{eq:main-DCS}) at $\boldsymbol{0}$ and using $\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{0})=1$
gives $D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{0})=\ln\!\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}^{2}_{i}]}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}]^{2}}\right]$
and $D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{Z},\boldsymbol{0})=\ln\!\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}^{2}_{i}]}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}_{i}]^{2}}\right].$
The trade-exposure weighted divergence between the consumption and
energy IO dependence vectors is
\begin{equation}
D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{a}^{Z})=\ln\!\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}^{2}_{i}]\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}^{2}_{i}]}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}\widehat{Z}_{i}]^{2}}\right].\label{eq:app-D-CZ}
\end{equation}
Subtracting (\ref{eq:app-D-CZ}) from the sum of $D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{0})$
and $D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{Z},\boldsymbol{0})$ yields 
\[
D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{0})+D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{Z},\boldsymbol{0})-D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{a}^{Z})=\ln\!\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}^{2}_{i}]}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}]^{2}}\right]+\ln\!\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}^{2}_{i}]}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}_{i}]^{2}}\right]-\ln\!\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}^{2}_{i}]\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}^{2}_{i}]}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}\widehat{Z}_{i}]^{2}}\right]=2\ln\!\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}\widehat{Z}_{i}]}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}]\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}_{i}]}\right].
\]
By the covariance definition, $\operatorname{Cov}_{i}(\widehat{C}_{i},\widehat{Z}_{i})\equiv\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}\widehat{Z}_{i}]-\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}]\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}_{i}]$,
we get $\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}\widehat{Z}_{i}]}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}]\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}_{i}]}=1+\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{i}(\widehat{C}_{i},\widehat{Z}_{i})}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}]\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}_{i}]}$.
Combining the above two equations yields the following
\begin{align}
2\ln\!\left[1+\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{i}(\widehat{C}_{i},\widehat{Z}_{i})}{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}]\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}_{i}]}\right]= & \ D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{0})+D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{Z},\boldsymbol{0})-D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{a}^{Z}).\label{eq:app-log-cov-identity}
\end{align}
Since $\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{C}_{i}]$ and $\mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{Z}_{i}]$
are strictly positive and the exponential function is strictly increasing,
we get
\begin{align}
\operatorname{Cov}_{i}(\widehat{C}_{i},\widehat{Z}_{i})>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad & D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{0})+D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{Z},\boldsymbol{0})>D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{a}^{Z}).\label{eq:app-sign-condition}
\end{align}
Next noting that $\mathbb{E}_{i}[\left(\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})\right)^{2}]=\operatorname{Var}_{i}(\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a}))+\mathbb{E}_{i}[\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})]^{2}$,
we can write the divergence between $\boldsymbol{a}$ and zero dependence
as $D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{0})=\ln\!\left[1+\operatorname{CV}_{i}(\Lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{a}))^{2}\right]$.
It thus follows that the denominator of the normalized divergence,
$D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{0})+D_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{Z},\boldsymbol{0})$,
is strictly positive if and only if at least some countries vary in
either their trade or consumption exposures to trade. Accordingly,
dividing (\ref{eq:app-sign-condition}) by the positive denominator
obtains the result under Remark 1:
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{Cov}_{i}(\widehat{C}_{i},\widehat{Z}_{i})>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{D}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{a}^{C},\boldsymbol{a}^{Z})<1,\label{eq:app-normalized-condition}
\end{equation}


\section{\label{sec: Optimal Transfer (app)}Required Transfers under Globally
Optimal Carbon Pricing}

\paragraph{Environment.}

Country $i$ faces a (possibly distorted) domestic consumer price
vector $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}_{++}$, and we write
$\tilde{\mathbf{P}}=(\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$. World
producer prices are analogously $\mathbf{P}$. Global emissions are
$Z\equiv Z^{(global)}\geq0$. Country $i$'s indirect utility is $V_{i}(E_{i},\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})$,
where $E_{i}$ is nominal expenditure (income after transfers) at
domestic consumer prices $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i}$. Welfare of country
$i$ is 
\begin{equation}
W_{i}=V_{i}(E_{i},\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})\Delta_{i}(Z),\label{eq:welfare}
\end{equation}
where $\Delta_{i}:\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{++}$ is the
climate-damage index. This is the indirect-utility version of the
welfare function in equation (\ref{eq:U_i})

\paragraph{Pareto weights and transfers.}

Fix Pareto weights $(\omega_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ with $\omega_{i}>0$
and $\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{i}=1$. Transfers are encoded by
expenditure shares $\alpha=(\alpha_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ on the
simplex, 
\[
\Lambda^{N}\equiv\left\{ \alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{+}:\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\alpha_{i}=1\right\} ,
\]
with national expenditure levels satisfying 
\begin{equation}
E_{i}=\alpha_{i}Y,\label{eq:Ei}
\end{equation}
where $Y$ is global income. Explicit international transfers are
therefore $T_{i}=E_{i}-Y_{i}$, where $Y_{i}$ is country $i$'s income
before the international transfer and includes the carbon-tax revenue
collected by that country. Transfer feasibility implies $\sum_{i}T_{i}=0$
and hence $\sum_{i}E_{i}=\sum_{i}Y_{i}=Y$.

\paragraph{Policies and income.}

A policy consists of prices of goods, including energy goods with
embedded carbon, $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}$, and transfers $\alpha$. Global
income is factor income plus the revenue from the goods-price wedges:
\begin{equation}
Y=\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\cdot\mathbf{L}+(\tilde{\mathbf{P}}-\mathbf{P})\cdot\mathbf{C}.\label{eq:Y}
\end{equation}
Here, $\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\cdot\mathbf{L}$ denotes world factor income
and $\mathbf{C}=(\mathbf{C}_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ is the vector
of quantities on which the goods-price wedges are levied.

\paragraph{Assumptions.}

Throughout we impose the following regularity conditions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textbf{A1.}] (\emph{Homotheticity and differentiability}) For each $i$, $V_{i}(\cdot,\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})$
is homogeneous of degree one in $E_{i}$, so 
\begin{equation}
V_{i}(E_{i},\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})=E_{i}V_{i}(1,\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i}),\qquad\frac{\partial\ln V_{i}(E_{i},\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})}{\partial\ln E_{i}}=1.\label{eq:hom}
\end{equation}
The underlying consumption aggregator is continuously differentiable
and homogeneous of degree one, and therefore satisfies 
\begin{equation}
\sum_{k\in\mathbb{K}}\frac{\partial C_{i}}{\partial C^{(H)}_{ik}}C^{(H)}_{ik}=C_{i}.\label{eq:consumption-euler}
\end{equation}
\item[\textbf{A2.}] (\emph{Climate damages}) Each $\Delta_{i}(Z)$ is positive and continuously
differentiable. At the optimum, the Pareto-weighted marginal effect
of global emissions is negative: 
\begin{equation}
\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{n}\frac{d\ln\Delta_{n}(Z)}{dZ}<0.\label{eq:aggregate-damage}
\end{equation}
No sign restriction is needed country by country.
\item[\textbf{A3.}] (\emph{Utility maximization}) For each $k\in\mathbb{K}$, Roy's identity
implies 
\begin{equation}
\frac{\partial\ln V_{i}(E_{i},\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})}{\partial\tilde{P}_{i,k}}=-\frac{\partial\ln V_{i}(E_{i},\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})}{\partial E_{i}}C^{(H)}_{ik}=-\frac{C^{(H)}_{ik}}{E_{i}}.\label{eq:roy}
\end{equation}
\item[\textbf{A4.}] (\emph{Cost minimization}) Producers minimize costs, profits are
exhausted in factor payments, and markets clear. The resulting income
envelope for each consumer-price coordinate is 
\begin{equation}
\frac{dY}{d\tilde{P}_{i,k}}=\big(C_{ik}-C^{(I)}_{ik}\big)+(\tilde{\mathbf{P}}-\mathbf{P})\cdot\frac{d\mathbf{C}}{d\tilde{P}_{i,k}}=C^{(H)}_{ik}+(\tilde{\mathbf{P}}-\mathbf{P})\cdot\frac{d\mathbf{C}}{d\tilde{P}_{i,k}}.\label{eq:income-envelope}
\end{equation}
Global emissions satisfy the corresponding accounting identity 
\begin{equation}
\frac{dZ}{d\tilde{P}_{i,k}}=\frac{dZ}{d\mathbf{C}}\cdot\frac{d\mathbf{C}}{d\tilde{P}_{i,k}}.\label{eq:emissions-envelope}
\end{equation}
\item[\textbf{A5.}] (\emph{Rank condition}) After fixing the numeraire, the matrix $D_{\tilde{\mathbf{P}}}\mathbf{C}$
of quantity responses to consumer prices has full rank at the optimum.
Economically, the available price changes generate enough independent
changes in quantities to identify the efficient price wedge.\bigskip{}
\end{enumerate}
\noindent\emph{Eisenberg--Gale program.}$\quad$Given Pareto weights
$\omega$, the program is 
\begin{equation}
\max_{\tilde{\mathbf{P}},\,\alpha\in\Lambda^{N}}\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{i}\ln W_{i}=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{i}\ln V_{i}(E_{i},\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})+\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{i}\ln\Delta_{i}(Z),\qquad\text{subject to }E_{i}=\alpha_{i}Y.\label{eq:EG}
\end{equation}
Transfers are implicitly determined by $\alpha$ through (\ref{eq:Ei}).

\bigskip{}
\noindent\emph{Optimal policy schedule.}$\quad$Under \textbf{A1--A5},
any interior solution $(\tilde{\mathbf{P}}^{*},\alpha^{*})$ to (\ref{eq:EG})
satisfies 
\begin{align}
\tilde{\mathbf{P}}^{*}-\mathbf{P}^{*} & =-Y^{*}\left[\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{n}\left.\frac{d\ln\Delta_{n}(Z)}{dZ}\right|_{Z=Z^{*}}\right]\left.\frac{dZ}{d\mathbf{C}}\right|_{\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}^{*}},\label{eq:free-trade}\\[4pt]
\alpha^{*}_{i} & =\omega_{i}\quad\forall i\in\mathbb{N},\qquad T^{*}_{i}=\omega_{i}Y^{*}-Y^{*}_{i}.\label{eq:alpha}
\end{align}
It is useful to write the efficient carbon price per ton as
\[
\tilde{\tau}^{*}\equiv-Y^{*}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{n}\left.\frac{d\ln\Delta_{n}(Z)}{dZ}\right|_{Z=Z^{*}}>0.
\]
Then equation (\ref{eq:free-trade}) is simply
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{P}}^{*}-\mathbf{P}^{*}=\tilde{\tau}^{*}\left.\frac{dZ}{d\mathbf{C}}\right|_{\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}^{*}}
\]


\paragraph{Optimal Policy Derivation.}

We proceed in two steps. The transfer condition is derived first because
it is the condition that makes the household-price terms cancel in
the price first-order condition.

\noindent\emph{Step 1 (optimal transfers).} At an efficient allocation
supported by consumer prices $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}^{*}$, including
the carbon wedge, the planner's first-order condition for every positive
household consumption quantity is
\begin{equation}
\omega_{i}\frac{\partial\ln C_{i}}{\partial C^{(H)}_{ik}}=\lambda\tilde{P}^{*}_{i,k},\label{eq:consumption-foc}
\end{equation}
where $\lambda>0$ is the common marginal value of nominal expenditure
and $\lambda\tilde{P}^{*}_{i,k}$ is the shadow cost of delivering
the good, inclusive of its marginal climate cost. Multiplying (\ref{eq:consumption-foc})
by $C^{(H)*}_{ik}$ and summing over $k\in\mathbb{K}$ gives
\begin{align}
\omega_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{K}}\frac{\partial\ln C_{i}}{\partial C^{(H)}_{ik}}C^{(H)*}_{ik}=\lambda\sum_{k\in\mathbb{K}}\tilde{P}^{*}_{i,k}C^{(H)*}_{ik},\qquad\qquad & \omega_{i}=\lambda E^{*}_{i}.\label{eq:transfer-euler}
\end{align}
The second line uses the Euler identity in (\ref{eq:consumption-euler})
and the budget constraint in equation (\ref{eq:Ei}). Summing (\ref{eq:transfer-euler})
over countries and using $\sum_{i}\omega_{i}=1$ and $\sum_{i}E^{*}_{i}=Y^{*}$
yields $1=\lambda Y^{*}$ and, thus, $\lambda=1/Y^{*}$. Therefore,
\begin{equation}
E^{*}_{i}=\omega_{i}Y^{*},\qquad\alpha^{*}_{i}=\omega_{i},\qquad T^{*}_{i}=E^{*}_{i}-Y^{*}_{i}=\omega_{i}Y^{*}-Y^{*}_{i},\label{eq:transfer-result}
\end{equation}
which proves (\ref{eq:alpha}).

\smallskip{}
 \noindent\emph{Step 2 (optimal prices).} By homotheticity in \textbf{A1},
$E_{i}=\alpha_{i}Y$, and $\sum_{i}\omega_{i}=1$, the planner's objective
can be written exactly as
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{i}\ln W_{i}=\  & \ln Y+\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{i}\ln\alpha_{i}+\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{i}\ln V_{i}(1,\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})+\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{i}\ln\Delta_{i}(Z).\end{aligned}
\label{eq:objective-decomposition}
\end{equation}
Fix $(i,k)$ and differentiate (\ref{eq:objective-decomposition})
with respect to $\tilde{P}_{i,k}$, holding the expenditure shares
fixed. This gives 
\begin{equation}
0=\frac{1}{Y}\frac{dY}{d\tilde{P}_{i,k}}+\omega_{i}\frac{\partial\ln V_{i}(1,\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})}{\partial\tilde{P}_{i,k}}+\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{n}\frac{d\ln\Delta_{n}(Z)}{dZ}\frac{dZ}{d\tilde{P}_{i,k}}.\label{eq:FOCgeneric}
\end{equation}
By \textbf{A1}, \textbf{A3}, and the transfer result $E^{*}_{i}=\omega_{i}Y^{*}$,
\begin{equation}
\omega_{i}\frac{\partial\ln V_{i}(1,\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{i})}{\partial\tilde{P}_{i,k}}=-\frac{\omega_{i}}{E_{i}}C^{(H)}_{ik}=-\frac{C^{(H)}_{ik}}{Y}\qquad\text{at the optimum}.\label{eq:roy-cancellation}
\end{equation}
Substituting (\ref{eq:income-envelope}), (\ref{eq:emissions-envelope}),
and (\ref{eq:roy-cancellation}) into (\ref{eq:FOCgeneric}) gives
\begin{align}
\frac{C^{(H)}_{ik}}{Y}+\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{P}}-\mathbf{P}}{Y}\cdot\frac{d\mathbf{C}}{d\tilde{P}_{i,k}} & -\frac{C^{(H)}_{ik}}{Y}+\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{n}\frac{d\ln\Delta_{n}(Z)}{dZ}\frac{dZ}{d\mathbf{C}}\cdot\frac{d\mathbf{C}}{d\tilde{P}_{i,k}}\nonumber \\
=\  & \left[\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{P}}-\mathbf{P}}{Y}+\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{n}\frac{d\ln\Delta_{n}(Z)}{dZ}\frac{dZ}{d\mathbf{C}}\right]\cdot\frac{d\mathbf{C}}{d\tilde{P}_{i,k}}=0.\label{eq:wedge-FOC-coordinate}
\end{align}
Collecting (\ref{eq:wedge-FOC-coordinate}) over all independent price
coordinates gives
\begin{equation}
\left[(\tilde{\mathbf{P}}^{*}-\mathbf{P}^{*})+Y^{*}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\omega_{n}\left.\frac{d\ln\Delta_{n}(Z)}{dZ}\right|_{Z=Z^{*}}\left.\frac{dZ}{d\mathbf{C}}\right|_{\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}^{*}}\right]D_{\tilde{\mathbf{P}}}\mathbf{C}(\tilde{\mathbf{P}}^{*},\alpha^{*})=0.\label{eq:wedge-FOC}
\end{equation}
By the rank condition in \textbf{A5}, the bracketed term must be zero.
Rearranging yields (\ref{eq:free-trade}). Together with Step 1, this
proves the optimal policy schedule.

\paragraph{Efficient carbon price along the supply chain.}

The price condition above determines the total charge on a ton of
carbon, but not the point along the supply chain at which that charge
is collected. For the two implementation results below, hold the pre-existing
ad valorem energy taxes at zero and consider the additive carbon prices
in equation (\ref{eq:carbon_wedge}). To state the result using the
notation of the main text, let $\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)}_{i}$ denote country
$i$'s uniform extraction-side carbon price, so $\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)}_{i,k}=\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)}_{i}$
for $k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}$, and let $\tilde{\tau}^{(C)}_{i}$ denote
its uniform demand-side carbon price, so $\tilde{\tau}^{(H)}_{i,k}=\tilde{\tau}^{(I)}_{i,kg}=\tilde{\tau}^{(C)}_{i}$
for energy uses covered by the tax.

Suppose carbon is counted once at extraction and once at combustion,
and is conserved as primary energy is traded and processed. Then every
positive flow of carbon extracted in country $j$ and ultimately burned
in country $i$ must face
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}_{j}+\tilde{\tau}^{(C)*}_{i}=\tilde{\tau}^{*}.\label{eq:chain-price}
\end{equation}
Thus efficiency fixes the total price per ton along the supply chain.
It does not require that the full amount be collected either at extraction
or at use.

The equalization across countries follows from simple comparisons.
If two extraction countries $j$ and $j'$ both supply carbon that
is burned in country $i$, then
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}_{j}+\tilde{\tau}^{(C)*}_{i}=\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}_{j'}+\tilde{\tau}^{(C)*}_{i}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}_{j}=\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}_{j'}.\label{eq:chain-price-extraction}
\end{equation}
If carbon extracted in country $j$ is burned in two countries $i$
and $i'$, then
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}_{j}+\tilde{\tau}^{(C)*}_{i}=\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}_{j}+\tilde{\tau}^{(C)*}_{i'}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\tilde{\tau}^{(C)*}_{i}=\tilde{\tau}^{(C)*}_{i'}.\label{eq:chain-price-combustion}
\end{equation}
If international energy trade overlaps sufficiently that all active
extraction and combustion countries are linked through positive energy
flows, these comparisons imply a common extraction-side component
and a common demand-side component:
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}_{j}=\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*},\qquad\tilde{\tau}^{(C)*}_{i}=\tilde{\tau}^{*}-\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*},\qquad0\leq\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}\leq\tilde{\tau}^{*}.\label{eq:chain-price-family}
\end{equation}
The pure demand-side scheme is the endpoint $\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}=0$;
the pure supply-side scheme is the endpoint $\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}=\tilde{\tau}^{*}$.
Under the carbon-accounting condition above, moving one dollar per
ton from the use side to the extraction side leaves the total charge
on every ton unchanged and therefore supports the same real allocation.
In this implementation, pre-tax producer prices and factor rewards
are unchanged; only the location of carbon-tax revenue changes.

\paragraph{Carbon-tax revenue in terms of emissions.}

The carbon-tax revenue component of country $i$'s income in equation
(\ref{eq:TaxRev_i}) can be written directly in terms of the location
of extraction and combustion. Under uniform additive carbon prices,
that revenue is
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)}_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}Z^{(Q)}_{i,k}+\tilde{\tau}^{(C)}_{i}Z_{i}.\label{eq:revenue-Z}
\end{equation}
The first term is revenue collected on carbon extracted in country
$i$; the second is revenue collected on carbon burned in country
$i$. Carbon accounting implies
\begin{equation}
\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}Z^{(Q)}_{i,k}=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}Z_{i}=Z.\label{eq:carbon-accounting-Z}
\end{equation}
Along the efficient family in (\ref{eq:chain-price-family}), world
carbon-tax revenue is therefore
\begin{align}
 & \sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\left[\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}Z^{(Q)*}_{i,k}+\big(\tilde{\tau}^{*}-\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}\big)Z^{*}_{i}\right]\nonumber \\
 & \qquad=\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}Z^{*}+\big(\tilde{\tau}^{*}-\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}\big)Z^{*}=\tilde{\tau}^{*}Z^{*}.\label{eq:world-revenue-Z}
\end{align}
Hence the location at which the efficient carbon price is collected
changes the distribution of revenue across countries, but not total
world revenue. Country $i$'s income along this family is 
\begin{align}
Y^{*}_{i}={} & w^{*}_{i}L_{i}+\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}r^{*}_{i,k}R_{i,k}+\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}Z^{(Q)*}_{i,k}+\big(\tilde{\tau}^{*}-\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}\big)Z^{*}_{i}\nonumber \\
={} & w^{*}_{i}L_{i}+\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}r^{*}_{i,k}R_{i,k}+\tilde{\tau}^{*}Z^{*}_{i}+\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}\left(\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}Z^{(Q)*}_{i,k}-Z^{*}_{i}\right),\label{eq:income-Z}
\end{align}
and the supporting international transfer remains 
\begin{equation}
T^{*}_{i}=\omega_{i}Y^{*}-Y^{*}_{i}.\label{eq:transfer-Z}
\end{equation}
Because the real allocation is the same at the two endpoints, factor
income and $Y^{*}$ are also the same. The transfer under the pure
supply-side implementation minus the transfer under the pure demand-side
implementation is therefore 
\begin{equation}
\left.T^{*}_{i}\right|_{\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}=\tilde{\tau}^{*}}-\left.T^{*}_{i}\right|_{\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)*}=0}=-\tilde{\tau}^{*}\left(\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}Z^{(Q)*}_{i,k}-Z^{*}_{i}\right).\label{eq:transfer-endpoints}
\end{equation}
Thus changing the point of collection redistributes revenue according
to the difference between carbon extracted in country $i$ and carbon
burned in country $i$. These differences sum to zero across countries.

\paragraph{Decentralization (Eisenberg--Gale).}

Given $\omega$, the program (\ref{eq:EG}) is a weighted Nash-product
maximization. Under the standard convexity conditions, its optimality
conditions coincide with the household, firm, market-clearing, and
budget conditions of a competitive equilibrium. Equation~(\ref{eq:free-trade})
provides the efficient goods-price wedge, while equation~(\ref{eq:alpha})
provides the lump-sum transfers that support $E^{*}_{i}=\omega_{i}Y^{*}$.
The efficient allocation is therefore supported as a decentralized
equilibrium. Equations~(\ref{eq:chain-price-family}) and (\ref{eq:transfer-endpoints})
show that the same allocation can be supported by any efficient split
of the carbon price between extraction and use, with the international
transfers adjusted for the resulting distribution of carbon-tax revenue.

\section{Equilibrium in Changes\label{sec:apdx-Eqlbrm_in_Changes}}

This section introduces the system of equations used to solve equilibrium
changes in response to trade and carbon policy shocks. Trade shocks
can arise from changes in iceberg trade costs, denoted as $d_{ij,k}$,
or from adjustments to trade taxes, import tariffs ($\tau^{(M)}_{ij,k}=1+t^{(M)'}_{ni,k}$)
or export taxes $(\tau^{(X)}_{ij,k}=1+t^{(X)}_{ij,k})$. Carbon policy
shocks, on the other hand, involve changes to supply-side taxes ($\tau^{(Q)}_{i,k}$)
that target carbon emissions at the point of primary energy extraction
$k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}$, and/or demand-side taxes that target carbon
emissions at the consumption location of primary or secondary energy
$k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}\cup\mathbb{E}_{2}$. These demand-side taxes are
applied to industries ($\tau^{(I)}_{i,kg}$) or households ($\tau^{(H)}_{i,k}$).

Note that in the main body of the paper, we did not explicitly model
import tariffs and export taxes $(\tau^{(M)}_{ij,k},\tau^{(X)}_{ij,k})$
on the trade policy side. Here, we include them for completeness.
In addition, to maintain generality in the model specification, below
we assume that the household consumption aggregator follows a CES
structure between energy (\emph{E}) and non-energy (\emph{N}) goods
with substitution elasticity $\eta_{H}$, with a Cobb-Douglas structure
within the energy and non-energy categories. Similarly, production
technologies are modeled as CES between energy (\emph{E}) and non-energy
(\emph{N}) with substitution elasticity $\eta_{I}$, with Cobb-Douglas
structures within each category. In our main specification, however,
we have adopted a simpler functional form with $\eta_{H}\rightarrow1$
and $\eta_{I}\rightarrow1$, which corresponds to a Cobb-Douglas aggregation
also over energy (\emph{E}) and non-energy (\emph{N}) goods.

To express equilibrium responses to trade and climate policy changes,
we adopt the exact hat algebra notation. For any generic variable
$z$ that denotes the value of $z$ in the status quo equilibrium,
we use $z'$ to denote its value in the counterfactual equilibrium,
with $\hat{z}\equiv z'/z$ representing the change from status quo
to the counterfactual value.

Consider a policy change that adjusts trade policy parameters to $\{d'_{ij,k},\tau^{(M)'}_{ij,k},\tau^{(X)'}_{ij,k}\}$
and carbon policy instruments to $\{t^{(Q)'}_{i,k},t^{(I)'}_{i,kg},t^{(H)'}_{i,k},\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)'}_{i,k},\tilde{\tau}^{(I)'}_{i,kg},\tilde{\tau}^{(H)'}_{i,k}\}$.

Prices along the supply chain include producer prices at the location
of supply, landed prices inclusive of production, export, and import
taxes, distribution-level prices that aggregate over landed price
in each destination, and consumer prices that additionally include
demand-side taxes. In our notation below, the cost share parameter
of natural resources, $\alpha^{R}_{i,k}$, is non-zero in the primary
energy industries and zero in all other industries. The change to
prices along the supply chain is as follows:
\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\widehat{P}_{ij,k}=\widehat{d}_{ij,k}\widehat{c}_{i,k} & \mbox{a) \text{producer price }}\\
\widehat{c}_{i,k}=\widehat{r}^{\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}_{i,k}\left(\delta^{E}_{i,k}\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}^{E}_{i,k}\right)^{1-\eta_{I}}+\left(1-\delta^{E}_{i,k}\right)\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}^{N}_{i,k}\right)^{1-\eta_{I}}\right)^{\frac{1-\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}{1-\eta_{I}}} & \text{b) \text{marginal cost }}\\
\hat{\tilde{P}}^{E}_{i,k}=\prod_{g\in\mathbb{E}}\hat{\tilde{P}}^{\delta^{E}_{i,kg}}_{i,kg},\:\:\:\hat{\tilde{P}}^{F}_{i,k}=\prod_{g\in\mathbb{F}}\hat{\tilde{P}}^{\delta^{F}_{i,kg}}_{i,kg},\:\:\:\hat{\tilde{P}}^{N}_{i,k}=\left(\hat{w}_{i}\right)^{\delta^{L}_{i,k}}\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}^{F}_{i,k}\right)^{1-\delta^{L}_{i,k}} & \text{ }\\
\widehat{\tilde{P}}_{ji,k}=\widehat{\tau^{(M)}_{ji,k}}\widehat{\tau^{(X)}_{ji,k}}\widehat{\tau^{(Q)}_{j,k}}\widehat{P}_{ji,k} & \text{c) landed price }\\
\widehat{\tilde{P}}_{i,k}=\left[\sum_{n}\lambda_{nj,k}\hat{\tilde{P}}^{1-\sigma_{k}}_{nj,k}\right]^{\frac{1}{1-\sigma_{k}}} & \mbox{d) distribution-level price}\\
\widehat{\tilde{P}}^{(I)}_{i,kg}=\hat{\tau}^{(I)}_{i,kg}\widehat{\tilde{P}}_{i,g},\:\:\:\widehat{\tilde{P}}^{(H)}_{i,g}=\hat{\tau}^{(H)}_{i,g}\widehat{\tilde{P}}_{i,g} & \mbox{e) consumer price}
\end{cases}\label{eq:price_hat}
\end{equation}
where $\delta^{E}_{i,kg}=\frac{\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}}{\sum_{g\in\mathbb{E}}\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}}$
is the cost share of each energy type out of total energy input costs,
$\delta^{F}_{i,kg}=\frac{\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}}{\sum_{g\in\mathbb{F}}\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}}$
is the cost share of each non-energy industry out of total non-energy
intermediate input costs, $\delta^{L}_{i,k}=\frac{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}}{\alpha^{L}_{i,k}+\sum_{g\in\mathbb{F}}\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}}$
is the cost share of labor out of total of labor and non-energy intermediate
inputs costs, and $\delta^{E}_{i,k}=\frac{\sum_{g\in\mathbb{E}}\alpha^{I}_{i,kg}}{1-\alpha^{R}_{i,k}}$
is the cost share of energy inputs out of total costs net of those
paid for carbon reserves.

The change in ad valorem carbon taxes on the supply and demand side
of fossil fuel markets are:
\[
\begin{cases}
\tau^{(Q)'}_{i,k}=\left(1+t^{(Q)'}_{i,k}\right)+\tilde{\tau}^{(Q)'}_{i,k}\frac{\hat{Z}^{(Q)}_{i,k}Z^{(Q)}_{i,k}}{\hat{Y}_{i,k}Y_{i,k}} & \:\:k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}\\
\tau^{(I)'}_{i,kg}=\left(1+t^{(I)'}_{i,kg}\right)+\tilde{\tau}^{(I)'}_{i,kg}\frac{\hat{Z}^{(I)}_{i,kg}Z^{(I)}_{i,kg}}{X^{(I)'}_{i,kg}} & \:\:k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}\cup\mathbb{E}_{2}\\
\tau^{(H)'}_{i,k}=\left(1+t^{(H)'}_{i,k}\right)+\tilde{\tau}^{(H)'}_{i,k}\frac{\hat{Z}^{(H)}_{i,k}Z^{(H)}_{i,k}}{X^{(H)'}_{i,k}} & \:\:k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}\cup\mathbb{E}_{2}
\end{cases}
\]

The change to international expenditure shares follow from the CES
gravity structure:
\begin{equation}
\widehat{\lambda}_{ij,k}=\left(\widehat{\tilde{P}}_{ij,k}\big/\widehat{\tilde{P}}_{j,k}\right)^{1-\sigma_{k}}\label{eq:lambda_hat}
\end{equation}
On the side of factor employment and intermediate input use, industries'
input cost shares are as follows:
\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\text{\ensuremath{\hat{\alpha}^{N}_{i,k}}\ensuremath{=\ensuremath{\frac{\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}^{N}_{i,k}\right)^{1-\eta_{I}}}{\delta^{E}_{i,k}\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}^{E}_{i,k}\right)^{1-\eta_{I}}+\left(1-\delta^{E}_{i,k}\right)\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}^{N}_{i,k}\right)^{1-\eta_{I}}}}}}, & \:\:\:\hat{\alpha}^{L}_{i,k}=\hat{\alpha}^{N}_{i,k},\qquad\hat{\alpha}^{I}_{i,kg}=\hat{\alpha}^{N}_{i,k}\:\:\:\text{for \ensuremath{g\in\mathbb{F}}}\\
\\\ensuremath{\hat{\alpha}^{E}_{i,k}}=\ensuremath{\frac{\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}^{E}_{i,k}\right)^{1-\eta_{I}}}{\delta^{E}_{i,k}\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}^{E}_{i,k}\right)^{1-\eta_{I}}+\left(1-\delta^{E}_{i,k}\right)\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}^{N}_{i,k}\right)^{1-\eta_{I}}},} & \:\:\:\hat{\alpha}^{I}_{i,kg}=\hat{\alpha}^{E}_{i,k}\:\:\:\text{for \ensuremath{g\in\mathbb{E}}}
\end{cases}\label{eq:alpha_hat}
\end{equation}

On the final consumption side, households' final expenditure shares
are given by:
\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\text{\ensuremath{\hat{\beta}^{N}_{i}}=\ensuremath{\left(\frac{\hat{\tilde{P}}^{N}_{i}}{\widehat{\tilde{P}}_{i}}\right)^{1-\eta_{H}}}} & \hat{\tilde{P}}^{N}_{i}=\prod_{k\in\mathbb{F}}\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,k}\right)^{\beta_{i,k|N}}\\
\ensuremath{\hat{\beta}^{E}_{i}}=\ensuremath{\left(\frac{\hat{\tilde{P}}^{E}_{i}}{\widehat{\tilde{P}}_{i}}\right)^{1-\eta_{H}}} & \hat{\tilde{P}}^{E}_{i}=\prod_{k\in\mathbb{E}}\left(\hat{\tilde{P}}_{i,k}\right)^{\beta_{i,k|E}}
\end{cases}\label{eq:beta_hat}
\end{equation}
where $\beta_{i,k|N}$ and $\beta_{i,k|E}$ denote cost shares within
the input bundles of non-energy and energy use. Changes to total sales,
$Y_{i,k}=P{}_{ii,k}Q{}_{i,k}$, in primary energy industries and
secondary and non-energy industries can be expressed as:
\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\widehat{Y}_{i,k}=\frac{1}{\hat{\alpha}^{R}_{i,k}}\widehat{r}_{i,k} & k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}\\
\widehat{Y}_{i,k}=\frac{1}{\hat{\alpha}^{L}_{i,k}}\widehat{\ell}_{i,k}\widehat{w}_{i} & k\in\mathbb{E}_{2}\cup\mathbb{F}
\end{cases}\label{eq:Y_hat}
\end{equation}
where $\ell_{i,k}=L_{i,k}/L_{i}$ denotes the employment share of
industry $k$ in country $i$. In the post-policy equilibrium, total
expenditures, inclusive or net of production and trade taxes, are
equal to:
\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\tilde{X}'_{i,k}=\overbrace{\frac{1}{\tau^{(H)'}_{i,k}}\hat{\beta}_{i,k}\beta_{i,k}\widehat{E}_{i}E_{i}}^{=X^{(H)'}_{i,k}}+\overbrace{\sum_{g\in\mathbb{E}\cup\mathbb{F}}\frac{1}{\tau^{(I)'}_{i,gk}}\hat{\alpha}^{I}_{i,gk}\alpha^{I}_{i,gk}\widehat{Y}_{i,g}Y_{i,g}}^{X^{(I)'}_{i,gk}},\\
\tilde{X'}_{ij,k}=\tilde{P}'_{ij,k}C'_{ij,k}=\hat{\lambda}_{ij,k}\lambda_{ij,k}\tilde{X}'_{i,k}\\
X'_{ij,k}=P'_{ij,k}C'_{ij,k}=\frac{\tilde{X'}_{ij,k}}{\tau^{(M)'}_{ij,k}\tau^{(X)'}_{ij,k}\tau^{(Q)'}_{i,k}}\\
X'_{j,k}=\sum_{i}X'_{ij,k}
\end{cases}\label{eq:X_hat}
\end{equation}
Using the changes in sales, expenditures, and prices, we can write
the changes in $\text{CO}_{2}$ emissions. Specifically, emissions
changes at different levels of aggregation are as follows:

\[
\begin{cases}
\widehat{Z}^{(I)}_{i,gk}=\frac{\hat{\alpha}^{I}_{i,kg}\hat{Y}_{i,k}}{\hat{\tilde{P}}^{(I)}_{i,gk}} & \mbox{a) industry emission }(i,k;\quad g\in\mathbb{E})\\
\widehat{Z}^{(H)}_{i,g}=\frac{\hat{\beta}_{i,g}\hat{E}_{i}}{\hat{\tilde{P}}^{(H)}_{i,g}} & \mbox{b) household emission }(i;\quad g\in\mathbb{E})\\
\widehat{Z}^{(I)}_{i}=\frac{1}{Z^{(I)}_{i}}\sum_{k}\sum_{g\in\mathbb{E}}\widehat{Z}^{(I)}_{i,gk}Z^{(I)}_{i,gk} & \mbox{c) industrial emission, }(i)\\
\widehat{Z}^{(H)}_{i}=\frac{1}{Z^{(H)}_{i}}\sum_{g\in\mathbb{E}}\widehat{Z}^{(H)}_{i,g}Z^{(H)}_{i,g} & \mbox{d) household emission, }(i)\\
\widehat{Z}_{i}=\frac{1}{Z_{i}}\left(\widehat{Z}^{(I)}_{i}Z^{(I)}_{i}+\widehat{Z}^{(H)}_{i}Z^{(H)}_{i}\right) & \text{e) national emission}\\
\widehat{Z}^{(global)}=\sum^{N}_{i=1}\left[\left(Z_{i}/Z^{\left(global\right)}\right)\times\widehat{Z}_{i}\right] & \mbox{f) global carbon emission}
\end{cases}
\]
Labor market clearing conditions equate the demand and supply of labor
at both the industry level and the national level, expressed in terms
of post-policy equilibrium values:
\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\hat{\ell}_{i,k}\ell_{i,k}w_{i}\hat{w}_{i}\bar{L}_{i}=\hat{\alpha}^{L}_{i,k}\alpha^{L}_{i,k}\sum_{j}X'_{ij,k} & \mbox{a) LMC }(i,k\in\mathbb{K})\\
\sum^{K}_{k=1}\hat{\ell}_{i,k}\ell_{i,k}=1 & \mbox{b) National LMC }(i)
\end{cases}\label{eq:MCC_Labor_hat}
\end{equation}

\begin{align}
\hat{r}_{i,k}r_{i,k}R_{i,k}= & \hat{\alpha}^{R}_{i,k}\alpha^{R}_{i,k}\sum_{j}X'_{ij,k},\qquad(i,k\in\mathbb{E}_{1})\label{eq:MCC_Energy_hat}
\end{align}
Lastly, the balance of budget requires that total final expenditure
equals the payments to factors of production plus the taxes that are
rebated to households:
\[
\widehat{E}_{i}E_{i}=\widehat{Y}_{i}Y_{i}+T'_{i},\qquad\widehat{Y}_{i}Y_{i}=\widehat{w}_{i}w_{i}L_{i}+\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}}\left[\widehat{r}_{i,k}r_{i,k}\bar{R}_{i,k}\right]
\]
where taxes consist of taxes at the points of local production, exports,
imports, and local demand
\[
T'^{(\text{demand})}_{i}=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}\cup\mathbb{E}_{2}}\left[\frac{\tau^{(H)'}_{i,k}-1}{\tau^{(H)'}_{i,k}}\hat{\beta}_{i,k}\beta_{i,k}\widehat{E}_{i}E_{i}+\sum_{g\in\mathbb{E}_{2}\cup\mathbb{F}}\frac{\tau^{(I)'}_{i,kg}-1}{\tau^{(I)'}_{i,kg}}\hat{\alpha}^{k}_{i,g}\alpha^{k}_{i,g}\widehat{Y}_{i,g}Y_{i,g}\right]
\]
\[
T'^{(\text{imports})}_{i}=\sum_{k}\sum_{n\neq i}\left[\frac{\tau^{(M)'}_{ni,k}-1}{\tau^{(M)'}_{ni,k}}\tilde{X}'_{ni,k}\right]
\]
\[
T'^{(\text{exports, supply})}_{i}=\sum_{k}\sum_{n}\left[\frac{\tau^{(Q)'}_{i,k}\tau^{(X)'}_{in,k}-1}{\tau^{(Q)'}_{i,k}\tau^{(X)'}_{in,k}\tau^{(M)'}_{in,k}}\tilde{X}'_{in,k}\right]
\]
\begin{align}
T'_{i}= & T'^{(\text{demand})}_{i}+T'^{(\text{imports})}_{i}+T'^{(\text{exports, supply})}_{i}\label{eq:T_hat}
\end{align}
where composite carbon tax rates, $\left\{ \tau^{(Q)'}_{i,k},\tau^{(I)'}_{i,kg},\tau^{(H)'}_{i,k}\right\} $
consist of additive and multiplicative terms following equation \ref{eq:carbon_wedge}
(evaluated at the post-policy equilibrium). 

\section{Climate Fund Based on Supply-side Carbon Taxes\label{sec:apdx-Climate-Fund-Supplyside}}

We formulate the optimal linkage problem described in Section \ref{subsec:linkage-with-transfers}
by considering the integration of \emph{supply-side} carbon taxes
into the WTO. This reform resembles the proposal presented in Section
\ref{subsec:Implementation-through-global-fund} of the main text,
but differs in two respects.

First, emissions are taxed at the point of primary energy extraction.
Second, the trade-related component of carbon-tax revenue is based
on the exported, rather than imported, share of that revenue. Formally,
the Fund satisfies the following global budget-balance condition:
\begin{align*}
\text{Fund} & =\sum_{i}\text{(contribution)}_{i}=\sum_{i}\text{(allocation)}_{i}\\
\text{where}\quad\text{(contribution)}_{i}=\text{(\text{carbon price})}_{i}\:\times\: & \sum_{k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}\cup\mathbb{E}_{2}}\left[\text{(exported share of expenditure)}_{i,k}\times Z^{(Q)}_{i,k}\right].
\end{align*}
Here, $Z^{(Q)}_{i,k}$ denotes the $\text{CO}_{2}$ emissions content
of primary energy $k\in\mathbb{E}_{1}$ (coal, crude oil, and natural
gas), and the exported share of expenditure measures the extent to
which the production of primary energy in a country is shipped to
the rest of the world through exports.

We solve this constrained-linkage problem by maximizing the carbon
price subject to constraints R1--R4, similar to the climate fund
based on demand-side taxes in our main specification.

Table \ref{tab:Fund_B1_Multi-SupplySide} presents the results. Without
transfers, the maximum carbon price is \$27/$\text{tCO}_{2}$. India
emerges as the marginal country, followed by Brazil and Pakistan.
Notably, these countries are neither the largest energy importers
nor the largest exporters; rather, they lie on an intermediate position.

Introducing a fund financed by the exported share of carbon-tax revenues
does not improve the outcome under any of the allocation rules considered.
Although the table examines more allocation rules than in the demand-side
design, none raises the maximum carbon price above \$27/$\text{tCO}_{2}$.
In almost all cases, Saudi Arabia becomes the marginal country at
very low carbon prices, typically followed by Russia.

These unfavorable outcomes arise because supply-side carbon tax revenues
are highly concentrated in major energy-producing countries that export
a large share of their energy production, such as Saudi Arabia and
Russia. On the one hand, this concentration makes the distributional
effects highly uneven without transfers. On the other hand, when transfers
are introduced based on the exported share of supply-side tax revenues,
the fund draws a disproportionately large share of its resources from
these major exporters, leaving them worse off. In short, extraction-tax
revenues are so unevenly distributed that they generate substantial
distributional effects; and attempts to offset those effects through
transfers lead to pushing the system to the opposite extreme by placing
an excessive burden on the largest exporters.
